entities.name: Mongol invasion of Central Asia
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Mongol invasion of Central Asia was a series of military campaigns (1209–1236) led by Genghis Khan's successors, including Ögedei Khan and Güyük Khan. This pivotal event took place in Central Asia, leaving a lasting impact on the region's politics, culture, and geography. It marked a significant turning point in the history of Central Asia, shaping the trajectory of the region for centuries to come.

The invasion began in 1216, when Ögedei Khan launched a campaign against the Khwarezmid Empire. The Mongols quickly conquered the empire's capital, Samarkand, and went on to capture other key cities, including Bukhara and Khiva. The campaign continued until 1221, when the Mongols finally defeated the Khwarezmid Empire.

The Mongol invasion had a profound impact on Central Asia, leading to the destruction of many cities and the displacement of countless people. It also had a lasting impact on the region's politics, as the Mongols established a network of trade routes and administrative centers that stretched from China to Eastern Europe. The invasion also had a significant cultural impact, as the Mongols spread Buddhism, Christianity, and Islam throughout the region.

The Mongol invasion of Central Asia was a defining moment in the history of the region, shaping the course of Central Asian history for centuries to come. One of the most striking legacies of the invasion was the establishment of the Golden Horde, a Mongol khanate that ruled over present-day Russia, Ukraine, and parts of Kazakhstan from the 13th to the 16th centuries.
